content: Posterior vaginal wall prolapse, also referred to as posterior compartment prolapse, can result in a sensation of vaginal bulging, obstructed defecation, and sexual dysfunction. Non-surgical management options include lifestyle modifications, pelvic floor muscle training, and pessary use. This review aimed to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of various surgical interventions for managing posterior vaginal wall prolapse. The review included 10 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1,099 women. The quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, with limitations primarily due to biases (performance, detection, and attrition) and imprecision caused by small sample sizes and low event rates. Transanal Repair vs. Transvaginal Repair: 1. Awareness of Prolapse: Women undergoing transanal repair were more likely to report awareness of prolapse compared to those undergoing transvaginal repair. If 10% of women are aware of prolapse after transvaginal repair, this figure could range from 10% to 79% after transanal repair (low-quality evidence). 2. Repeat Surgery for Prolapse: There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in repeat surgery rates between the two groups (low-quality evidence). 3. Recurrent Posterior Vaginal Wall Prolapse: Recurrent prolapse was more likely after transanal repair. If 10% of women experience recurrent prolapse after transvaginal repair, this could range from 16% to 100% after transanal repair (moderate-quality evidence). 4. Postoperative Obstructed Defecation: Obstructed defecation was more common following transanal repair (low-quality evidence). 5. Postoperative Dyspareunia: There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in rates of dyspareunia between the two groups (moderate-quality evidence). 6. Postoperative Complications: No conclusive evidence was found to suggest differences in complication rates between the two groups. If 2% of women experience complications after transvaginal repair, this could range from 2% to 21% after transanal repair (low-quality evidence). 7. Operating Time: There was no clear difference in operating time between the two approaches (very low-quality evidence). Biological Graft vs. Native Tissue Repair: 1. Awareness of Prolapse: There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in awareness of prolapse between the two groups (moderate-quality evidence). 2. Repeat Surgery for Prolapse: Evidence was insufficient to show differences in repeat surgery rates (moderate-quality evidence). 3. Recurrent Posterior Vaginal Wall Prolapse: There was no conclusive evidence of differences in recurrence rates. If 13% of women experience recurrent prolapse after native tissue repair, this could range from 4% to 13% after biological graft repair (moderate-quality evidence). 4. Postoperative Obstructed Defecation: Evidence was insufficient to determine differences in rates of obstructed defecation (moderate-quality evidence). 5. Postoperative Dyspareunia: There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in dyspareunia rates (low-quality evidence). 6. Postoperative Complications: Complications were more common with biological graft repair (low-quality evidence). Other Comparisons: Single RCTs compared various surgical techniques, including site-specific vaginal repair versus midline fascial plication, absorbable graft versus native tissue repair, synthetic graft versus native tissue repair, and levator ani plication versus midline fascial plication. However, data were limited, and no definitive conclusions could be drawn regarding the relative effectiveness or safety of these interventions. The mesh exposure rate in the synthetic graft group was 7%. Authors' Conclusions: Transvaginal repair appears to be more effective than transanal repair in reducing the recurrence of posterior wall prolapse, based on both objective and subjective measures. However, data on adverse effects were limited. There was insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about the relative effectiveness or safety of other surgical techniques. The findings do not support the routine use of mesh or graft materials during posterior vaginal wall repair. Additionally, the withdrawal of some commercial transvaginal mesh kits from the market may limit the applicability of these findings.
